name: Newspaper
disposalMethod: Place in your blue recycling bin. Keep dry — wet paper cannot be recycled. Remove any plastic wrappers before recycling.

name: Cardboard Box
disposalMethod: Flatten all boxes before placing in the recycling bin. Remove any tape, labels, or foam inserts. Keep dry.

name: Coffee Cup
disposalMethod: Most coffee cups have a plastic lining and cannot be recycled in standard paper bins. Check for specialised coffee cup collection points at cafes.

name: PET Water Bottle (Code 1)
disposalMethod: Rinse thoroughly, remove the cap and label if possible, then crush and place in recycling. Code 1 plastics are widely accepted.

name: Plastic Bag
disposalMethod: Do NOT place in curbside recycling — plastic bags jam sorting machinery. Return to supermarket collection points or switch to reusable bags.

name: HDPE Milk Jug (Code 2)
disposalMethod: Rinse well and place in your recycling bin. Code 2 plastics are among the most widely recycled — accepted at most facilities.

name: Polystyrene (Styrofoam)
disposalMethod: Not accepted in curbside recycling. Look for specialised drop-off points. Alternatively, minimise purchase of products packaged in polystyrene.

name: Glass Bottle
disposalMethod: Rinse and place in your glass recycling bin. Remove lids (recycle metal lids separately). Broken glass should be wrapped in newspaper before disposal for safety.

name: Glass Jar
disposalMethod: Remove the lid and rinse the jar. Metal lids can go in the metal recycling. Place the jar in the glass bin — both clear and coloured glass are accepted.

name: Broken Glassware
disposalMethod: Drinking glasses and Pyrex/oven-safe dishes have different melting points than bottle glass and cannot be recycled together. Wrap safely and place in general waste.

name: Aluminium Can
disposalMethod: Rinse and place in your recycling bin. Aluminium can be recycled indefinitely with only 5% of the energy needed to produce new aluminium. Always recycle!

name: Steel Food Tin
disposalMethod: Rinse thoroughly and place in recycling. Steel tins are 100% recyclable and highly valuable to the recycling industry. No need to remove labels.

name: Aerosol Can
disposalMethod: Ensure the can is completely empty — never puncture or crush. Empty aerosols are accepted in most metal recycling. Check your local guidelines.

name: Food Scraps
disposalMethod: Compost in a home compost bin or food waste collection caddy. Avoid composting meat, fish, and dairy in open compost bins to prevent pests.

name: Garden Waste
disposalMethod: Place in your garden waste bin, home compost, or take to a green waste facility. Grass clippings, leaves, and small branches are all compostable.

name: Teabags
disposalMethod: Many teabags contain plastic mesh and should go in general waste. Look for brands with plastic-free, compostable bags — these can be composted whole.

name: Smartphone
disposalMethod: Never put in regular bins — smartphones contain toxic lithium, mercury, and lead. Return to a certified e-waste facility, mobile network store, or manufacturer take-back scheme.

name: Laptop / Computer
disposalMethod: Erase all personal data first. Take to a certified e-waste recycler, electronics retailer drop-off, or donate if still functional. Do not place in household bins.

name: Batteries (AA/AAA)
disposalMethod: Household batteries contain toxic chemicals. Drop off at supermarket battery collection points, electronics retailers, or hazardous waste facilities. Never landfill.

name: Printer Cartridge
disposalMethod: Many manufacturers and office supply stores offer free cartridge return schemes. Some charities also collect cartridges for fundraising. Never place in general waste.
